description: Hi! We are a friendly, ambitious team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge in Astana.
summary: What if your Moon lander touched down in perfect shape, then lost power because a mountain blocked the Sun? Lunar Landing Site Navigator prevents that: it combines JPL Horizons and LOLA terrain data to show, in seconds, where and when a south-pole landing gets both sunlight and a direct link to Earth, with 3D views anyone can understand.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that shows, in seconds, whether a lunar landing site and date give a lander sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth.

How it works: the user picks a site (NASA's Artemis III candidate regions, commercial and international landings, Apollo, or custom coordinates) and a date. The app gets Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons and computes the real terrain horizon from LRO LOLA elevation data, then gives a verdict: sunlight share, Earth link share, longest darkness, Sun elevation and time until sunset and Earthset. Results are shown as a sky chart, 3D terrain with shadows, a horizon panorama, an animated timeline, a year-long planner and a side-by-side comparison. Checked at the Apollo sites: within 0.02° for the Sun and 0.22° for the Earth.

Impact: near the south pole one crater rim or a short launch delay can make a site unusable. The app helps mission planners re-check sites and dates fast, and helps students and the public understand why.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, Tailwind CSS, JPL Horizons API, LOLA data via USGS. Developed with the help of an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic).

We focused on accuracy (real terrain, Apollo validation), clarity (beginner and expert modes) and use on any device.
